system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2146-05-16 14:34:00 to 2146-05-21 18:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, and long QT syndrome, was admitted for nausea and vomiting lasting two days, possibly triggered by grapefruit ingestion or recent Bactrim use. He was found to have pre-renal acute kidney injury with elevated creatinine, which improved with IV fluids. A urine culture confirmed Proteus mirabilis infection, and he was treated with a full course of Bactrim. He developed a mild pruritic rash after a dose of ceftriaxone, which resolved with Benadryl. His nausea improved with Ativan and hydration, and he tolerated oral intake by discharge. He was discharged home with antibiotics, instructions to resume G-tube feeds, and plans for outpatient follow-up including urine testing and EKG for QT monitoring.

cardioversion in past) colon cancer s/p resection in ___ G tube needed for

COMPARISON:  CT dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ Interventional ___ and Dr.
___, Interventional Radiology fellow performed the procedure. Dr.
___ supervised the trainee during any key components of the
procedure where applicable and reviewed and agrees with the findings as
reported below.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
150mcg of fentanyl and 1.5 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 43 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: None.
CONTRAST: 10 ml of Optiray contrast
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  10.3 minutes, 49 mGy

PROCEDURE:  16 ___ mic gastrojejunostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

The existing tube was injected with contrast and showed opacification of
duodenum.  The stay sutures were cut and a stiff roadrunner wire was
introduced into duodenum.  A second secured exchange wire was also placed. 
The existing feeding tube was then removed.  The tube was exchanged over the
stiff roadrunner.  The gastric balloon was inflated and retracted towards the
skin.  Contrast was injected to confirm appropriate placement in the stomach
and duodenum after removal of the roadrunner.  After confirmation of
appropriate placement the safety wire was removed.

The catheter was then flushed, capped and secured to the skin with 0-silk
sutures. Sterile dressings were applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS:


1. The retained GJ tube appears to have partially broken off of the distal
portion.
2. 2 wires are seen within the distal duodenum exiting through a lateral wall
break through the indwelling GJ tube.
3. Appropriately positioned new 16 ___ mic gastrojejunostomy tube.

Successful exchange of a gastrojejunostomy tube for a new 16 ___ mic
gastrojejunostomy tube. The tube is ready to use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having abdominal pain and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve had this constant pain near my belly button for about two days now. And I’ve had five loose stools today—no blood, but it’s worse than my usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice—dark green vomit. I couldn’t keep my meds down yesterday, including my transplant pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chest pain. Just the belly pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of C. diff and liver transplant, we need to be careful. We’ve started some fluids and gave you Zofran for nausea. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff before. This feels similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re checking your stool. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen to rule out blockages or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the CT safe with my heart condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We avoid certain medications due to your long QT, but imaging is fine. The scan showed no blockage or perforation—your transplant liver looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. My G-tube has been clogged too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Nutrition is helping with Ensure for now. We’ll plan to replace the tube if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My blood pressure’s usually okay—why is it so high now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from pain and stress. We’ll monitor it. If it stays high, we may start a mild medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back positive for C. diff—both the PCR and toxin tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s what’s causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Even though the CT didn’t show colitis, the positive toxin means we should treat it. We’re starting oral vancomycin—125 mg four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interact with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s safe with your transplant meds. We’ve held loperamide and opium tincture for now—they can worsen C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll skip those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up to 2.4—likely from not eating or drinking much. We’re giving some IV fluids to help your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damage getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like temporary stress from dehydration. Your levels were 1.5 on admission and should improve with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on Ensure—will I get tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend it, but you can decide. We’ll replace the clogged tube soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is improving, and you’re keeping food down. Creatinine is already down to 1.8—great response to fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Interventional radiology will replace it tomorrow. It’s a quick procedure under light sedation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be drowsy but breathing on your own. We’ll use medications safe for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray shows a small fluid collection on the right side—likely from reduced movement. It’s not pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s common in hospitalized patients. Deep breathing and walking will help clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. You need to finish a few more days of vancomycin. We also want to make sure your blood pressure stays down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, consistently above 150. We’re starting amlodipine 5 mg daily. Your PCP will adjust it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your G-tube was successfully replaced this morning. It’s ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it go well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The old tube was damaged, which caused the clog. The new one is secure. Home health will help with feeds after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try feeds at home, but I’m not sure I want them long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll support whatever you choose. Nutrition will send instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last labs show creatinine back to 1.5, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds do I take home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds except loperamide and opium tincture—they stay on hold. Add vancomycin for 14 days and amlodipine daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart feeds at home. A nurse will visit to help set it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Keep taking vancomycin until the end of the course, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any warning signs to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call if diarrhea returns severely, or if you have fever, belly swelling, or can’t keep fluids down. Also monitor your weight—call if you gain or lose more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Your PCP may check an EKG in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your team soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing—should I restart my pain meds fully?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue oxymorphone and hydromorphone as needed. Use the lidocaine patch and gabapentin too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely—keep taking mycophenolate and prednisone every day. Do not skip them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—vancomycin four times a day, amlodipine once daily, and no loperamide until diarrhea resolves?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And weigh yourself daily, low-salt diet, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, malnutrition, and congenital long QT syndrome, was admitted for abdominal pain and acute-on-chronic diarrhea. He reported symptoms similar to prior C. difficile infection. CT scan showed no obstruction or colitis, but stool testing confirmed C. difficile with positive PCR and toxin. Oral vancomycin was started for a 14-day course. His G-tube was clogged on admission, leading to supplemental nutrition; it was successfully exchanged on hospital day 4. Creatinine rose to 2.4 due to poor oral intake but improved to baseline with IV fluids. Blood pressure remained elevated, prompting initiation of amlodipine. He was discharged home with services to continue tube feeds, complete antibiotics, and follow up with his primary team.
